title: Afterburner: kernel one-offs and quick mitigations (PM shift)
body:
PM shift quick scratchpad — evening run

Context:
- short window during PM shift where a handful of customer requests hit a path that triggers cold KV-cache lookups + long attention lengths.
- saw p99 jump to ~1.8s on the hosted endpoint for a few minutes. source: datadog span traces + sampling.

Observed timeline (rough):
- 18:07: spike begins (alerts fired), p95 stable ~200ms, p99 ~1.8s
- 18:09 one pod OOM-killed (looks like transient memory pressure)
- 18:11 autoscaler added 1 instance, traffic rebalanced, p99 back to ~300ms
- 18:15 alerts resolved (no further OOMs)

Quick reproduction steps I ran (local-ish):
- curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -H 'Authorization: Bearer test' -d @payload-heavy-attn.json
- run micro-bench: ./tools/send-burst --profile heavy_attn --concurrency 8 --seq-len 2048
- repro sometimes correlates with repeated reranks + long context (~>1600 tokens)

Spot findings / hypotheses:
1) KV-cache eviction thrash: a few large requests evict small prefix caches for many concurrent requests. evictions + reloads cause spikes.
2) GPU mem fragmentation after OOMs causes slower kernel allocation for ~10–20s window.
3) Scheduler starve: when instance took a cold batch, batching window increased from 5ms -> 40ms due to continuous batching backpressure from long sequences.

Evidence snippets:
- dmesg excerpts around the OOM: 
  [ 18:09:03 ] dev/gpu0: driver: mem alloc failed, fallback to host=1
  [ 18:09:06 ] container: pid 7623 oom-kill event
- trace id X: root span shows +1.2s on kv_cache::fetch_many (hot key miss)

Quick mitigations attempted during shift (what worked / what didn't):
- temporary route throttling for endpoint /generate-heavy -> success: lowered p99 back within SLO, but customer latency impacted.
- applied per-pod mem soft-limits -> prevented subsequent OOMs but introduced more swap (not ideal).
- set KV_CACHE_EVICTION_THRESHOLD=0.15 -> reduced thrash in short term, need to test wider impact.

Immediate TODOs (low friction):
- [ ] add temporary circuit-breaker that bypasses KV cache for >1500 token requests (config flag) — quick toggle in console. (owner: Sylvia)
- [ ] run controlled load test with combinations: seq-len {512,1536,2048} x concurrency {1,8,16} and capture kv miss rate + allocation latency. (owner: Ishan)
- [ ] create a small benchmark for fragmentation: spawn allocate/free cycles to simulate OOM -> measure allocation latency recovery. (owner: Noor)

Longer-term work items / experiments:
- instrument per-request KV-cache occupancy + eviction reason telemetry (metrics + tag on traces). goal: understand which keys are causing churn.
- experiment: proactive prefix pinning for requests with repeat prefixes (detect via LRU signature) — reduces repeated reloads.
- revisit batching window heuristics: if avg seq-len in batch > 1200, reduce batching window to 1ms to avoid batch head-of-line blocking.
- look into cudaMalloc defragmentation strategy or forced small-alloc warmups after OOMs. open question: safe to force a sequence of small allocations on warmup?

Notes to self (small tips and commands):
- quick trace: curl to /debug/trace?sample=1 with trace header to get span ids for datadog.
- to check eviction: redis-cli --scan | xargs redis-cli memory usage <key> (careful in prod)
- reproduce GPU mem fragmentation: ./tools/gpu-frag-sim --alloc-sizes "1G,200M,50M" --cycles 200

Slack / ask list:
- @noor: can you try changing KV_CACHE_EVICTION_THRESHOLD to 0.1 on staging and run renew load?
- @ishaan: can you add a micro-benchmark that logs allocation latency per-request? need percentile view.
- @infra: any recent kernel upgrades on hosts in us-west-2-g? suspect driver noise.

Followup items for post-mortem (if this becomes a ticket):
- collect full traces for all affected request IDs between 18:05–18:20
- compare memory map snapshots pre/post OOM across pods
- timeline of deploys/changes around 18:00 (did not see a deploy but double-check)
- decide on fallback policy: warmup small allocs vs retry vs bypass cache for long seqs

Random quick heuristics I scribbled during triage:
- if p99 >> p95 and spike is short (<5m) then check for OOMs and autoscaler activity first
- watch for correlated increases in redis MISS_RATE and batch-window-ms

Open questions (need triage):
- Is it worth adding a per-request kv-cache bypass flag at SDK level so customers can opt-in on heavy requests? tradeoffs: more tokens, more unit-cost but stable latency.
- How sensitive is the model kernel to small allocation bursts after OOM? (need bench)

Next-day plan:
- run the controlled load matrix in staging, collect metrics (kv miss, alloc latency, batch window, p99)
- add a short-lived server-side feature flag to bypass kv-cache for super-long requests and evaluate for 24h on a small percentage of traffic
- draft a short status update for the oncall channel and open JIRA if we see recurrence

End notes: felt less like a kernel bug and more like a cross-layer interaction (cache + batching + memory). prioritize telemetry first so we can avoid knee-jerk patching.

---
Small log append (18:50): noticed a second tiny spike when a bunch of reranks (N=16) hit the route simultaneously. probably same root cause.

-- S.P.
